If either name, http-equiv, or itemprop is specified in meta element, then the content attribute must also be specified.
If "responsive-embedded-sizing" is specified to value of name attribute of mata element, what is specfied to value of content attribute of this meta element?

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-meta-element

> If either name, http-equiv, or itemprop is specified, then the content attribute must also be specified. Otherwise, it must be omitted.

But just below:

> If a meta element has a name attribute, it sets document metadata.... If a meta element has no content attribute, then the value part of the metadata name-value pair is the empty string.

So `meta` with `name` and without `content` is allowed (but, imho it's a bit confusing for HTML to use must in "this must be specified, otherwise it must not be specified" instead of may?)

> If a meta element has no content attribute, then the value part of the metadata name-value pair is the empty string.

The above specifications are for user agents, not for authors.
Regardless of how the user agent processes it, author must comply with the following specifications.

> If either name, http-equiv, or itemprop is specified, then the content attribute must also be specified.

@annevk can you help whether the `content` attribute is required or not? It looks to me that omitting is allowed from what @miketaylr quoted, but I'm not sure.

@mtrootyy wrote:
> > If a meta element has no content attribute, then the value part of the metadata name-value pair is the empty string.
> 
> The above specifications are for user agents, not for authors. Regardless of how the user agent processes it, author must comply with the following specifications.
>

Is there good coverage for adding/removing the meta tag dynamically before <body> is seen?

@noamr 
> the tests link points to existing tests in wpt.fyi that are not marked tentative.

I removed `.tentative` because the template of this PR requested me to do so, there's a [CSS WG resolution](https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/1771#issuecomment-3806716273), and the resolution is put in the [CSS spec](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-sizing-4/#iframe-frame-sizing). With this discussion, I will make sure the CSS spec is updated. Was that too early?

> Is there good coverage for adding/removing the meta tag dynamically before is seen?

Yes, I think so, though they're based on the previous understanding of the "immutable" in the CSS WG. Among the [wpt tests](https://wpt.fyi/results/css/css-sizing/responsive-iframe?label=master&label=experimental&aligned):
* `meta-in-body` tests `<meta>` appearing in `<body>`.
* `meta-afterr-head` tests `<meta>` in after-head insertion mode.
* `dynamic-append` tests appending `<meta>`.
* `dynamic-remove` tests removing `<meta>`.
* `dynamic-write` tests `document.write`.
* `dynamic-name-change` tests changing the `name` attribute.

I'll update/add tests and Blink once this discussion is settled down.

WHATNOT notes/minutes:

Responsive Iframe Meta Tag Proposal: Noam Rosenthal introduced a proposal (PR 12444) to add a meta tag for responsive embedded sizing, which serves as an opt-in for parents to resize iframes. Luke questioned if domain-specific opt-ins are necessary, but Simon Pieters noted that CSP frame ancestors already provide existing protections. The group discussed whether the meta tag provides sufficient control over cross-origin information access, with Noam Rosenthal comparing the functionality to an explicit post-message opt-in.

Responsive Iframe Data Leakage Concerns: The group discussed potential privacy risks, specifically whether responsive iframes could allow an origin to infer information about a user (e.g., whether they are logged into a site) based on size changes. Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that the CSS working group previously discussed these risks and deemed them manageable if the parent page manages the sizing. Simon Pieters raised concerns regarding how to handle navigations and potential data leakage between pages.

Responsive Iframe Implementation and Documentation: Luke suggested that browsers should provide console warnings if an iframe opts into this feature without appropriate frame ancestor restrictions. Noam Rosenthal committed to updating the security explainer for the PR and consulting with Koji to ensure privacy concerns are addressed. Philip Jägenstedt clarified that fence frames, while still present in Chromium code, are not currently being actively developed.

I got another feedback from our security folks to add `allowed-origin` attribute. The value syntax is similar to [`frame-ancestors`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/frame-ancestors), but also allows wildcard. Examples:
```
<meta name="responsive-embedded-sizing" allowed-origins="https://example.org/ https://example2.org/">
<meta name="responsive-embedded-sizing" allowed-origins="*">
```
/cc @emilio @smfr
This PR is updated to include the `allowed_origins` attribute mentioned above.

<details><summary>AI Review</summary>

Reviewed at `8fd9d89`. The algorithm reads cleanly and all cross-references resolve (`starts with`, `set create`, `split on ASCII whitespace`, `serialization of an origin`, the two new CSP imports, `refsCSSSIZING`). It mirrors the `referrer` processing model and the CSP `frame-ancestors` navigation response check closely, which is the right template. Remaining points, roughly in order of importance:

### Cross-spec consistency with css-sizing-4

The CSS side (§ HTML iframe details) currently disagrees with this PR in four ways, and I think at least (3) is new since the last round:

1. When the flag becomes false — CSS: "if the `body` element is opened … during the initial document parse"; here: on `reveal`. (Known; already discussed.)
2. CSS calls the third state "unset", here it's null; and CSS defines its own `Document/responsive embedded sizing flag`, which should become a reference to the exported HTML dfn once this lands.
3. **CSS says `<meta name=responsive-embedded-sizing>` alone opts in** (its example at L1305 has no `content`). Under this PR, a `meta` with no `content`, or a `content` not starting with `allow-origins=`, is a no-op, so the CSS example never opts in. Worth calling out explicitly in the CSSWG follow-up, since it's an author-visible change in the opt-in syntax, not just a timing refinement.
4. `requestResize()` throws when the flag is "unset or false" — fine with this PR, just needs the terminology sync.

Suggest linking the csswg-drafts PR from the OP so they land together.

### What "reveal" implies for the opt-in window

`reveal` runs from *update the rendering* only for `docs` that survive "Filter non-renderable documents" and "Unnecessary rendering" — so a document in a hidden tab, a prerendered document, a render-blocked document, or one the UA chooses to skip is never revealed until that changes. Consequences:

- Script can set the flag to true arbitrarily late in such documents (after `body`, after `load`), unlike the parse-bounded rule in CSS.
- CSS reads the flag "when it performs a layout"; forced layouts (e.g. `getBoundingClientRect()`) can run before reveal, so CSS will observe a null→true transition after layouts have already happened. That's probably fine given the ICB lock is only recorded when the flag is true, but it should be a conscious decision and the CSS text ("will not change its value again") updated to match.
- `document.open()` doesn't reset the flag (nor `has been revealed`), so a re-opened document keeps the earlier true/false. Consistent with the revealed design; just confirming it's intended.

None of this is necessarily wrong — it is consistent with how render-blocking is bounded — but the PR description/commit message should state the model ("fixed at first rendering update") since it's the thing implementers will test against. @zcorpan's thread about resetting the *locked embedded ICB size* on navigation still looks open; that's a CSS-side formalization but is the other half of the leak argument.

### `'self'` / `'none'` semantics

`sourceList` is matched with *document*'s origin as the CSP `origin` argument, so `'self'` means "embedder is same-origin with this document". That's a sensible meaning but nothing in the authoring text says so; `ancestor-source-list` also admits `'none'`, which here is just a verbose way to not opt in. Suggest a sentence in the `<dd>` (and perhaps a second example) spelling out `'self'`.

### Content value robustness

- `starts with "allow-origins="` is case-sensitive and whitespace-sensitive. Other standard metadata names are tolerant (`referrer` lowercases; `color-scheme`/`theme-color` go through CSS parsing with whitespace skipping). At minimum, I'd `strip leading and trailing ASCII whitespace` from *value* before the prefix check — `content=" allow-origins=…"` silently failing is a footgun. Whether the key is case-insensitive should be stated either way.
- Is `allow-origins=` intended to be the only key forever? If future keys are plausible, defining the value as whitespace- or `;`-separated `key=value` tokens now avoids a breaking parse change later. Question, not a blocker.

### Editorial

- Document section: "set to false when revealing the Document" → "set to false, if still null, when revealing…" to match the step.
- "allows a document to opt in to responsively-sized iframes when embedded by an allowed container origin" — the subject is the embedded document; maybe "allows a document, when embedded in an `iframe` by a page from one of the listed origins, to opt in to being responsively sized."
- The conformance paragraph "There must not be more than one `meta` element … per document" — "per document" reads oddly at the end; the `theme-color` wording ("There must not be more than one `meta` element with its `name` attribute set to … per document") puts it the same way, so fine to keep for consistency.
- `tokens` holds a list after splitting; "Let *tokens* be the substring of *value* …, split on ASCII whitespace" is OK but "Let *tokens* be the result of splitting the code unit substring of *value* from the length of "`allow-origins=`" to the end on ASCII whitespace" is closer to how Infra phrases it. Nit.
- Example `<pre>` continuation line is indented 6 spaces inside the `<code>`; that whitespace renders. Compare the single-line `theme-color` examples.

</details>
